title: How Rabies Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain rabies: a viral disease that attacks the central nervous system, its history (Mesopotamian dog laws, St. Hubert, Louis Pasteur's vaccine), how the virus travels to the spinal cord and brain and then to the salivary glands, the furious and paralytic forms, transmission routes (bites, rare aerosol in bat caves, corneal transplant cases), animals most associated with rabies (raccoons, bats, dogs), symptoms in animals and humans, hydrophobia, global deaths and vaccination efforts, Bali and Hawaii rabies-free status, the Milwaukee protocol after Jeanna Giese's survival, and the Ozzy Osborne bat story. The episode also includes a sponsor read at the start, a Squarespace-style ad, and a listener mail about a man whose eyeball was forced out during water skiing.

segments.title: Opening banter and Old Yeller
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, a Squarespace sponsor read, and a joke about Old Yeller dying of rabies, then introduce the topic.

segments.title: Rabies history and Pasteur's vaccine
segments.summary: Rabies is found on every continent except Antarctica and is very old. Mesopotamian laws on rabid dogs, the word's Latin and French origins, pilgrimages to St. Hubert in Liege, and Louis Pasteur's vaccine developed in 1885 through trials based on introducing weakened virus.

segments.title: How rabies attacks the body
segments.summary: Rabies is a viral disease that attacks the central nervous system. The virus travels along nerves to the spinal cord and brain, replicates in neurons, then moves to the salivary glands, the main route of transmission. The virus is considered fatal once it reaches the central nervous system.

segments.title: Furious and paralytic forms of rabies
segments.summary: The two forms of rabies, furious (encephalitic) and paralytic (dumb), both occur in the acute stage and can occur in the same case. Discussion of which form the virus takes depending on where it lodges.

segments.title: Animals, bats, raccoons and transmission risk
segments.summary: Rabies affects only mammals. Wild rabid animals lose fear of humans. A New Jersey boy was attacked by a raccoon. Small mammals rarely survive to carry the disease. Saliva is the main transmission route; feces and blood are not. Aerosol transmission occurred in a Texas bat cave. Other possible but uncommon routes include kissing, sexual contact, and corneal transplant. Testing requires examining the animal's brain.

segments.title: Signs of rabies in animals
segments.summary: Symptoms in animals include paralysis, loss of appetite, nocturnal animals out during the day, excessive drooling, lack of fear of humans, pica, mood changes, and disorientation. Bats are the main rabies transmission vector in the US, and bat bites can go unnoticed.

segments.title: Rabies-free places, pet vaccination, and global deaths
segments.summary: Bali lost its rabies-free status in 2008 after dogs spread the virus. Hawaii uses strict quarantine. US wildlife services use oral vaccine baits for raccoons. Pet vaccination laws have nearly eliminated dog rabies in the US. Worldwide, tens of thousands die yearly, mostly in developing countries.

segments.title: Human symptoms, hydrophobia, and survival cases
segments.summary: Early human symptoms include stomach pain, anxiety, and fever, progressing to hallucinations, delirium, and coma. Hydrophobia is an intense fear of water caused by painful throat spasms. Gina Geise survived after being put into a medically induced coma, leading to the Milwaukee protocol. Peruvian groups showed some natural immunity.

segments.title: Old rabies treatment and Ozzy Osborne
segments.summary: The old series of 20 to 23 abdominal shots used from the 1950s to mid-1980s. The Ozzy Osborne bat-biting incident is discussed, and the hosts consider getting vaccinated.

segments.title: Listener mail: eyeball popped out water skiing
segments.summary: A listener describes her father's eyeball being forced out of its socket while water skiing in Las Vegas and pushed back in; he never saw a doctor and recovered vision in six months. Hosts close with credits and a search tip for howstuffworks.
